title: Monetary Policy
outcomes: Define monetary policy and describe its framework — objectives, transmission (analytics) and operating procedure.
Explain the channels of monetary transmission: saving–investment (interest rate), cash-flow, asset price and wealth, exchange rate and credit channels.

Explain quantitative tools (CRR, SLR, OMO, bank rate, LAF — repo, reverse repo, MSF — and MSS) and qualitative tools (margin requirements, moral suasion, selective credit control), with the current rates quoted in the study material.
Describe India's flexible inflation targeting framework and the Monetary Policy Committee — the 2016 amendment, the 4% ± 2% CPI target, and what counts as failure.

meta.exam_tip: Know the direction of every tool (tight vs easy money), the definitions (repo = RBI lends against securities; reverse repo = RBI borrows), the MPC (6 members, majority vote) and the target (CPI 4% with 2%–6% band; failure = average outside the band for three consecutive quarters). Quote the rates given in your study material: repo 5.25%, MSF 5.50%, reverse repo 3.35%, CRR 3%, SLR 18%.

concepts.title: Introduction and definition of monetary policy
body: The RBI periodically changes policy rates to steer liquidity and explains why. Monetary policy is how the central bank tries to stabilise the economy.

Monetary policy is the central bank's use of its instruments to influence how much money and credit is available, what it costs and how it is used, in order to promote growth, price stability, optimum output and employment, balance-of-payments equilibrium, a stable currency or other goals of economic policy.

The RBI uses it mainly to achieve price stability — low and stable inflation — while supporting growth. It adjusts money supply, typically by buying or selling securities in the open market, which changes short-term interest rates; these in turn affect long-term rates and activity.
Lowering interest rates = easing (accommodative) policy; raising them = tightening.
concepts.analogy: Monetary policy is the economy's water valve: open it (cheaper, more money) when growth is dry, tighten it when prices are flooding.
concepts.work: Every RBI policy announcement changes loan EMIs, deposit rates and bond prices — CAs in banks, treasuries and wealth management react the same day.

concepts.title: The monetary policy framework and its objectives
body: Three components: (i) objectives; (ii) analytics — the transmission mechanism; (iii) operating procedure — operating targets and instruments.

The RBI Act, 1934 (preamble) sets the aim: to regulate the issue of bank notes and keep reserves to secure monetary stability, and to operate the currency and credit system to the country's advantage. The core objective has been a sensible balance between price stability and growth.

Developing countries add explicit objectives: sustaining growth, adequate credit to productive sectors, a moderate interest-rate structure to encourage investment, and an efficient government securities market. With a more open economy and financial reforms, financial stability and exchange-rate stability have gained importance in India.
Worldwide, the most common objectives today are price stability (controlling inflation) and growth.
concepts.analogy: Like a car with two goals — reaching quickly (growth) and safely (stable prices): the driver must balance speed and control.
concepts.work: Bank ALCO meetings begin with the RBI's stated stance and objectives, because they decide the direction of rates for the bank's assets and liabilities.

concepts.title: Transmission of monetary policy — the channels
body: Transmission is how changes in policy settings flow through to activity and inflation, in two stages: policy changes affect interest rates; interest rates affect spending and inflation. The timing and size of effects are uncertain and lagged.

Saving and investment (interest-rate) channel: lower deposit rates reduce the reward for saving and encourage spending; lower loan rates encourage households to borrow (supporting demand for housing and other assets) and firms to invest, as projects more easily beat the cost of borrowing — especially firms that rely on debt. A contractionary rate rise does the reverse: it raises the cost of capital and real borrowing costs for firms and households.

Cash-flow channel: lower lending rates cut interest payments, leaving more cash for spending — important for liquidity-constrained borrowers (e.g. floating-rate home loans). Lower deposit income may make some savers spend less, but the first effect is larger, so spending rises overall.

Asset prices and wealth channel: lower rates raise asset prices (housing, shares) because future income is discounted at a lower rate; higher asset values increase collateral and make borrowing easier; higher wealth raises consumption and housing investment.

Exchange rate channel: if Indian rates fall relative to the rest of the world, Indian assets become less attractive, capital moves out and the rupee depreciates; exports become more competitive and imports dearer, raising activity — and also inflation through import prices. Most important for export-oriented and import-competing sectors.

Credit channels: the bank lending channel (policy changes alter banks' ability and willingness to lend) and the balance sheet channel (policy changes the net worth and cash flows of firms and households, and so their access to credit). Some texts call these the quantum channel.

Effect of a rate CUT
rows: Less saving, more borrowing, more investment
Lower EMIs leave more cash to spend
Higher house and share prices, more collateral, more spending
Rupee weakens → exports rise, imports dearer, some inflation
Banks lend more; stronger borrower balance sheets
blocks.title: Transmission channels

concepts.analogy: A rate change is a stone dropped in a pond; the channels are the different ripples reaching different shores — savers, borrowers, asset owners and exporters.
concepts.work: Since rates on most new bank loans are linked to an external benchmark like the repo rate, CAs in lending firms see transmission directly in EMIs.

concepts.title: Operating procedure — quantitative tools
body: Quantitative tools affect money supply across the whole economy — manufacturing, agriculture, housing, autos and so on.

Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR): the share of net demand and time liabilities (NDTL) a scheduled commercial bank must keep as cash with the RBI, whatever its size. It earns nothing and cannot be lent. CRR = 3% (as on 5 August 2026). A CRR cut releases funds and expands credit — used in deflation or slowdown; a hike absorbs funds.

Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR): the share of NDTL that banks must hold themselves in cash, gold or approved securities such as government securities; these earn some (low) interest. SLR = 18% (as on 5 August 2026).

Open Market Operations (OMO): the RBI buys or sells government securities in the market to adjust rupee liquidity. Selling securities absorbs liquidity (anti-inflationary — used to control inflation); buying injects liquidity (used in a slowdown or liquidity shortage). Exam note: the study material says sales suck liquidity out and purchases do the opposite, but its next sentence, as printed, attaches "to control inflation" to purchases — a slip. In the exam, link OMO sales with controlling inflation and OMO purchases with easing. OMOs also smooth temporary liquidity mismatches, for example from foreign capital flows.

Market Stabilisation Scheme (MSS): to absorb surplus liquidity (typically from large capital inflows), the Government issues additional treasury bills or dated securities over and above its normal borrowing; the proceeds are kept in a separate account with the RBI.
concepts.analogy: CRR is money locked in the RBI's safe; SLR is money the bank must keep in its own safe in specified forms; OMO is the RBI's sponge — squeezing in or soaking up liquidity.
concepts.work: Bank treasurers compute daily CRR and SLR positions; a shortfall attracts a penalty linked to the bank rate.

concepts.title: Policy rates — bank rate and the Liquidity Adjustment Facility
body: Bank rate: the standard rate at which the RBI is prepared to buy or rediscount bills of exchange or other eligible commercial paper — in practice the rate for longer-term funds. Today it is mainly used to set penalties for banks that fall short of CRR or SLR; the RBI steers money supply chiefly through the LAF repo rate. (The bank rate is aligned to the MSF rate.)
Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF): introduced on the recommendations of the Narasimham Committee on banking reforms; through it the RBI adjusts day-to-day liquidity via repos and reverse repos.

Repo (repurchase agreement): banks borrow short-term funds from the RBI by selling government securities with an agreement to buy them back at a set price and date — collateralised lending. The fixed overnight repo rate under LAF is the policy rate. Repo rate = 5.25% (as on 5 August 2026).

Reverse repo: the RBI borrows from banks (absorbs liquidity) by selling them securities with an agreement to repurchase; the rate the RBI pays banks for parking surplus funds. Reverse repo rate = 3.35% (as on 5 August 2026).

Marginal Standing Facility (MSF): a penal window where scheduled banks borrow overnight over and above LAF by dipping into their SLR securities up to a limit (the material says a maximum of 1% of SLR securities; under current RBI operating rules a bank may dip into SLR holdings up to 2% of its NDTL for MSF). MSF rate = 5.50% (as on 5 August 2026), i.e. 0.25 percentage point above repo. Older texts give the relations MSF = repo + 1 and reverse repo = repo − 1; quote the current figures in the exam.

For awareness (beyond the material): since April 2022 the floor of the corridor is the Standing Deposit Facility (SDF), at 0.25 percentage point below repo; the fixed-rate reverse repo at 3.35% continues alongside.

blocks.title: Policy rates and ratios quoted in the study material

concepts.analogy: Repo is a pawn-shop loan: the bank hands over bonds, takes cash, and buys the bonds back tomorrow. Reverse repo is the bank lending its spare cash to the pawn-shop owner (RBI).
concepts.work: Bank treasuries choose between the repo window, the inter-bank call market and MSF every day; MSF use signals tight liquidity.

concepts.title: Qualitative (selective) tools
body: Qualitative tools affect credit to specific sectors rather than total money supply.
Margin requirements: the RBI prescribes the margin a borrower must bring against collateral; raising margins reduces how much can be borrowed (e.g. against shares or commodities).
Moral suasion: persuasion by the RBI — letters, meetings, speeches — urging banks to lend to or avoid certain sectors.
Selective credit control: restricting credit to particular industries or speculative activities.
concepts.analogy: Quantitative tools change the size of the river; qualitative tools dig channels that send water to some fields and not others.
concepts.work: Higher margins on loans against shares or gold directly change how much a client can borrow — a practical point in wealth advisory.

concepts.title: Organisational structure — MPC and flexible inflation targeting
body: The RBI Act, 1934 was amended (effective 27 June 2016) to put the Monetary Policy Framework Agreement (MPFA) on a legal footing and to create a Monetary Policy Committee (MPC). The MPFA is an agreement between the Government and the RBI on the maximum tolerable inflation the RBI should target; the amended Act provides the statutory basis for flexible inflation targeting.

Inflation targeting means announcing an official target range for inflation. The Expert Committee under Urjit Patel (January 2014) recommended dropping the "multiple indicator" approach and making inflation targeting the primary objective.

The Government, in consultation with the RBI, sets the target once every five years. It notified CPI inflation of 4% with an upper tolerance of 6% and a lower tolerance of 2% for 5 August 2016 to 31 March 2021; the same target was retained for April 2021 to March 2026.
Failure to meet the target: average inflation above the upper tolerance level for any three consecutive quarters, or below the lower tolerance level for any three consecutive quarters.
Twice a year (every six months) the RBI must release a Monetary Policy Report setting out where inflation is coming from and its forecasts for the next six to eighteen months.

CPI was chosen because it reflects the cost of living and strongly influences inflation expectations. India thus joined countries such as New Zealand, the US, the UK, the euro area and Brazil; some countries are now considering nominal GDP targeting.

The MPC has six members: the RBI Governor (chairperson), the Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy, one RBI officer nominated by the Central Board, and three external members appointed by the Central Government. It sets the policy repo rate needed to reach the target by debate and majority vote; the Governor has a casting vote in a tie.

Detail
rows: Government in consultation with RBI, every 5 years
Average outside the band for 3 consecutive quarters
6 members; majority vote; Governor's casting vote
blocks.title: Flexible inflation targeting in India

concepts.analogy: The government sets the thermostat (4% ± 2%); the MPC is the committee that turns the dial (repo rate) to keep the room within that range.
concepts.work: Economists in banks and corporates forecast each MPC decision from CPI prints relative to the 4% target and the 6% upper band.

concepts.title: Conclusion — why monetary policy is hard
body: Choosing a policy action is complicated by uncertainty and the need to balance growth and inflation.

Emerging markets like India face extra problems: rudimentary and non-competitive financial systems, poorly integrated money and inter-bank markets, external uncertainties, and limits to the central bank's operational autonomy. Inflation is also driven by oil and food prices, which monetary policy cannot control directly.
Explicit inflation targeting needs operational autonomy for the central bank and good coordination between fiscal and monetary authorities.
concepts.analogy: Steering a ship in fog with a delayed rudder: you act on today's readings, but the turn happens months later.
concepts.work: Interest-rate risk management in companies (hedging, fixed vs floating debt) exists precisely because monetary policy outcomes are uncertain.

solution.text: A 0.5 point CRR cut releases 0.5% × 10,00,000 = ₹5,000 crore of lendable funds.

illustrations.title: Cost of overnight borrowing: repo vs MSF
illustrations.q: A bank needs ₹500 crore overnight. Find the interest cost (₹ lakh, 365-day year) under repo at 5.25% and under MSF at 5.50%. Another bank parks ₹500 crore overnight under reverse repo at 3.35%; find its income.

solution.text: MSF costs ₹0.34 lakh more per night — a penalty for not planning liquidity.

illustrations.title: The policy corridor
illustrations.q: Using the rates in the study material, find the gap between MSF and repo, and between repo and reverse repo.

solution.text: MSF − repo = 5.50 − 5.25 = 0.25 percentage point; repo − reverse repo = 5.25 − 3.35 = 1.9 percentage points. Overnight inter-bank rates normally stay between the floor and the MSF ceiling, close to the repo rate.

illustrations.title: Has the RBI failed to meet the target?
illustrations.q: Quarterly average CPI inflation: Case A — 6.4%, 6.8%, 6.2% in three consecutive quarters. Case B — 6.9%, 5.8%, 6.5%. Has the inflation target been missed in each case?

solution.text: Case A: every one of three consecutive quarters is above 6% (average of the three 6.47%) → failure; the RBI must report reasons and remedial actions to the Government.
Case B: the middle quarter (5.8%) is within the band, so there are not three consecutive quarters above 6% (even though the three-quarter mean is 6.4%) → not a failure under the rule.

jobs.title: Floating-rate loan after a repo hike
jobs.situation: The MPC raises the repo rate by 0.25%; the client's working-capital loan is linked to repo.
steps: Explain transmission: the external benchmark rate rises, so the loan rate rises by the same margin at reset.
Compute the extra annual interest on the average outstanding balance.
Review options — faster collections, cheaper trade credit, or fixing part of the borrowing.
jobs.takeaway: Policy decisions reach firms quickly through benchmark-linked loans.
jobs.think: Which transmission channel is this mainly?
jobs.answer: The cash-flow channel (and the saving–investment/interest-rate channel): higher repayments leave less cash to spend and make new investment costlier.

jobs.title: Treasury liquidity plan
jobs.situation: Large tax outflows will drain liquidity next week.
steps: Plan to borrow under repo/LAF using surplus SLR securities rather than the costlier MSF.
Keep CRR compliant every day to avoid penalties linked to the bank rate.
jobs.takeaway: Knowing the corridor (repo, MSF, reverse repo) saves real money.

jobs.title: Reading an MPC statement for clients
jobs.situation: The MPC holds the repo rate but changes its stance to neutral.
steps: Note CPI relative to the 4% target and 2–6% band.
Explain implications for bond prices and fixed-deposit rates.
jobs.takeaway: The inflation-targeting framework gives a clear yardstick for interpreting decisions.

mcqs.q: Monetary policy refers to the use of instruments by the central bank to regulate:
options: How much money and credit is available, its cost and its use
mcqs.explain: Monetary policy means the central bank using its tools to control how much money and credit is available, what it costs and where it goes, in order to achieve goals such as price stability and growth. 'Government spending and taxation' is the trap — that is fiscal policy, run through the budget. In practice: when RBI changes the repo rate, bank lending rates, EMIs and deposit rates adjust, which treasury teams and CAs factor into financing decisions.

mcqs.q: When the central bank lowers interest rates, monetary policy is said to be:
mcqs.explain: Lowering interest rates makes borrowing cheaper and encourages spending and investment, so the stance is described as easing (accommodative). 'Tightening' is the trap — that means raising rates to restrain demand and inflation. In practice: when RBI's MPC cut the repo rate during 2019–20, banks reduced home-loan and corporate lending rates, and analysts described policy as easing.

mcqs.q: The main objective of monetary policy in India is:
options: Price stability while keeping in mind the objective of growth
mcqs.explain: Under India's flexible inflation targeting framework, the RBI's primary objective is price stability while keeping in mind the objective of growth. 'Fixing the exchange rate' is the trap — India has a market-determined exchange rate, and the RBI only intervenes to curb excessive volatility. In practice: MPC resolutions always discuss CPI inflation against the 4% target alongside the GDP growth outlook.

mcqs.q: The three components of the monetary policy framework are:
mcqs.explain: The monetary policy framework has three parts: objectives (what policy aims at), analytics or transmission (how policy affects the economy), and the operating procedure (targets and instruments used day to day). 'Taxes, spending and borrowing' is the trap — those are fiscal tools; CRR, SLR and OMO are only some instruments. In practice: the RBI's Monetary Policy Report explains each of these elements to markets.

mcqs.q: The monetary transmission mechanism refers to:
options: The channels through which policy changes affect output and prices
Printing and distribution of currency notes
Transfer of RBI surplus to the government
mcqs.explain: The monetary transmission mechanism is the set of channels — interest rates, credit, asset prices, exchange rate and expectations — through which a change in policy affects aggregate demand, output and inflation. 'Printing and distribution of currency notes' is the trap: that is currency management, not transmission. In practice: RBI often comments on how fully repo-rate changes have passed through to bank lending rates.

mcqs.q: A contractionary policy-induced rise in interest rates:
options: Raises the cost of capital and real borrowing costs for firms and households
Raises borrowing costs only for firms
mcqs.explain: A policy-induced rise in interest rates raises the cost of capital and real borrowing costs for both firms and households, reducing investment and spending on homes, cars and consumer durables. 'Raises borrowing costs only for firms' is the trap — households with home and personal loans are hit too. In practice: after repo hikes, banks raise rates on repo-linked home loans, so borrowers' EMIs or tenures increase.

mcqs.q: Lower interest rates raising share and house prices and thus consumption is the:
mcqs.explain: Lower interest rates raise the value of shares and property; as people feel wealthier and their collateral improves, they consume and borrow more — the asset price and wealth channel. 'Cash-flow channel' is the trap: that works through borrowers' interest payments, not asset values. In practice: Indian equity and housing markets often rally after RBI rate cuts, lifting consumer spending through this channel.

mcqs.q: A cut in Indian interest rates relative to world rates tends to:
options: Depreciate the rupee, boost exports and add to inflation
Appreciate the rupee and cut exports
mcqs.explain: If Indian interest rates fall relative to world rates, foreign capital becomes less attracted, the rupee tends to depreciate, exports become cheaper abroad and imports costlier at home — adding to inflation. 'Appreciate the rupee and cut exports' is the trap, which reverses the effect. In practice: exporters' CFOs watch RBI rate decisions, because rupee movements change their competitiveness and the rupee value of their earnings.

mcqs.q: The Cash Reserve Ratio is maintained by banks:
options: As cash with the RBI, as a share of NDTL
In government securities held by the bank
mcqs.explain: The Cash Reserve Ratio is the share of a bank's net demand and time liabilities (NDTL) kept as cash balances with the RBI; it earns no interest. 'In government securities held by the bank' is the trap — that describes SLR, which banks hold themselves. In practice: bank treasury teams compute the CRR requirement on their NDTL each reporting fortnight to avoid penalties.

mcqs.q: The SLR as on 5 August 2026 (per the study material) is (in %):
mcqs.explain: Per the study material, as on 5 August 2026 the Statutory Liquidity Ratio is 18% of NDTL, held in liquid assets such as government securities, cash and gold. The tempting 3% is the CRR; 24% is an older SLR level. In practice: bank treasuries hold at least 18% of NDTL in approved government securities, which is a steady source of demand in India's G-sec market.

mcqs.q: The CRR as on 5 August 2026 (per the study material) is (in %):
mcqs.explain: Per the study material, as on 5 August 2026 the Cash Reserve Ratio is 3% of NDTL, kept as cash with the RBI. The tempting 18% is the SLR; 5.25% is the repo rate, a policy rate rather than a reserve ratio. In practice: every percentage-point change in CRR changes the funds banks can lend by about 1% of total NDTL, so CRR cuts free up substantial liquidity.

mcqs.q: During deflation the RBI would typically:
options: Reduce CRR so banks can expand credit
mcqs.explain: In deflation, demand and prices are falling, so the RBI wants banks to lend more; reducing the CRR frees cash banks can lend. 'Raise CRR to expand credit' is the trap — a higher CRR locks up more funds and contracts credit. Selling securities also drains liquidity. In practice: the RBI cut the CRR during the 2020 Covid slowdown to release funds to banks.

mcqs.q: NDTL of a bank is ₹10,00,000 crore; CRR 3%, SLR 18%. Funds available for lending are:
mcqs.explain: CRR = 3% × 10,00,000 = 30,000; SLR = 18% × 10,00,000 = 1,80,000. Funds available for lending = 10,00,000 − 30,000 − 1,80,000 = ₹7,90,000 crore. Traps: ₹9,70,000 crore deducts only CRR; ₹8,20,000 crore deducts only SLR; ₹2,10,000 crore is the total locked up. In practice: bank ALM teams start from NDTL and reserve requirements when planning lending capacity.

mcqs.q: To absorb excess liquidity from the market, the RBI will:
mcqs.explain: To absorb excess liquidity, the RBI sells government securities in open market operations; banks pay for them from their reserves, draining liquidity. 'Buy government securities' is the trap — purchases inject liquidity. Cutting CRR or repo would also add liquidity. In practice: when capital inflows flood the system, the RBI uses OMO sales and other tools to mop up excess funds.

mcqs.q: An open market operation involves buying or selling of:
mcqs.explain: Open market operations are the RBI's purchases and sales of government securities in the market to manage liquidity and money supply. 'Shares and debentures of companies' is the trap — the RBI does not conduct OMOs in corporate securities. In practice: RBI's OMO purchase announcements typically push G-sec yields down, which bond dealers at banks and mutual funds watch closely.

mcqs.q: Under the Market Stabilisation Scheme:
options: The government issues additional T-bills/securities to absorb surplus liquidity, the proceeds being held with the RBI
Banks borrow overnight from the RBI
The RBI cuts the repo rate
mcqs.explain: Under the Market Stabilisation Scheme, the government issues extra treasury bills or dated securities to absorb surplus liquidity, and the proceeds are held in a separate account with the RBI rather than spent. It is used mainly to sterilise large capital inflows. 'Banks borrow overnight from the RBI' is the trap — that is a repo or MSF transaction. In practice: MSS was used heavily in 2004–08 and after demonetisation in 2016.

mcqs.q: Under which facility does the RBI provide accommodation to banks through repos and reverse repos?
mcqs.explain: Under the Liquidity Adjustment Facility, the RBI injects liquidity by lending to banks through repos and absorbs it through reverse repos, against government securities. The Market Stabilisation Scheme is the trap — it uses government securities issuance to absorb liquidity, not repo windows. In practice: bank treasuries use LAF windows daily to manage their short-term funding gaps.

mcqs.q: In India the "policy rate" is:
options: The fixed overnight repo rate under the LAF
mcqs.explain: In India, the policy rate is the fixed overnight repo rate under the LAF, set by the Monetary Policy Committee; it signals the monetary policy stance. 'The bank rate' is the trap — it is now mainly used for penalties. The MSF rate is a penal ceiling above repo, and CRR is a reserve ratio, not a rate. In practice: home-loan EBLR rates in India are linked directly to the repo rate.

mcqs.q: A reverse repo operation takes place when:
options: The RBI borrows from banks by giving them securities
Banks borrow from the RBI against securities
Banks borrow from each other overnight
The RBI lends to the government
mcqs.explain: In a reverse repo, the RBI borrows from banks by giving them government securities, with an agreement to buy them back — it absorbs surplus liquidity. 'Banks borrow from the RBI against securities' is the trap — that is a repo, which injects liquidity. In practice: when banks have surplus funds, they park them with the RBI through reverse repo or the Standing Deposit Facility.

mcqs.q: Per the study material (5 August 2026), the repo rate is (in %):
mcqs.explain: Per the study material, as on 5 August 2026 the repo rate is 5.25%. The tempting 5.5% is the Marginal Standing Facility rate, and 3.35% is the reverse repo rate given in the same material. In practice: banks benchmark repo-linked loans to this rate, so a change of even 0.25 percentage point moves EMIs for millions of borrowers.

mcqs.q: Banks borrowing overnight beyond LAF by dipping into SLR securities use the:
mcqs.explain: The Marginal Standing Facility lets banks borrow overnight from the RBI at a penal rate above the repo rate, even by dipping into their SLR securities within a limit. 'Reverse repo window' is the trap — that is for depositing surplus funds with the RBI, not borrowing. In practice: banks use MSF only when they face a sudden shortfall, such as during advance-tax outflows, because it is costlier than repo.

mcqs.q: A bank borrows ₹500 crore for one night under MSF at 5.50% (365-day year). The interest cost in ₹ lakh is about:
mcqs.explain: Interest = principal × rate × days ÷ 365 = 500 crore × 5.50% × 1 ÷ 365 = ₹0.0753 crore = ₹7.53 lakh. Traps: 7.19 uses the repo rate of 5.25%; 4.59 uses the reverse repo rate of 3.35%; 27.5 is a full year's interest in crore, not one night's in lakh. In practice: bank treasurers compute such overnight costs when choosing between funding windows.

mcqs.q: Today the bank rate is mainly used to:
options: Set penalties for shortfalls in CRR/SLR
mcqs.explain: Today the RBI uses the repo rate as its operating policy rate; the bank rate is mainly used to set penal interest when banks fall short of their CRR or SLR requirements. 'Determine the daily policy stance' is the trap — that role belongs to the repo rate. In practice: compliance teams at banks track the bank rate because CRR/SLR shortfall penalties are calculated with reference to it.

mcqs.q: Raising the margin requirement on loans against shares is a:
mcqs.explain: Raising the margin requirement on loans against shares means borrowers get less credit for the same collateral, targeting credit for a particular use (share speculation) — a qualitative or selective tool. 'Quantitative tool' is the trap: quantitative tools, like CRR and OMO, affect total money supply across the economy. In practice: margin rules for loans against shares and gold are set by regulators to prevent speculative excess.

mcqs.q: Persuading banks through meetings and letters to restrict lending to a sector is called:
mcqs.explain: Moral suasion is the RBI persuading banks — through meetings, letters and speeches — to follow its wishes, such as restricting lending to a sector, without legal compulsion. 'Open market operation' is the trap: that is a quantitative tool that buys or sells securities. In practice: RBI Governors often use public speeches and meetings with bank CEOs to nudge them on lending standards or rate transmission.

mcqs.q: The Monetary Policy Committee consists of:
options: Six members and decides by majority vote
Five members and decides by consensus of the Governor
Twelve bankers chosen by the Finance Ministry
mcqs.explain: The Monetary Policy Committee has six members — three from the RBI, including the Governor, and three external members appointed by the government — and decides by majority vote, with the Governor having a casting vote in a tie. 'Five members deciding by the Governor's consensus' is the trap. In practice: MPC minutes show how each member voted, which market analysts study for clues on future rate moves.
mcqs.topic: The Organisational Structure for Monetary Policy Decisions

mcqs.q: The Monetary Policy Framework Agreement is an agreement on:
options: The maximum tolerable inflation the RBI should target
The maximum repo rate for government borrowing
mcqs.explain: The Monetary Policy Framework Agreement, between the Government of India and the RBI, sets the maximum tolerable inflation the RBI should target for price stability; the 2016 amendment to the RBI Act gave it statutory backing. 'The maximum repo rate for government borrowing' is the trap — the agreement fixes an inflation target, not interest rates. In practice: the agreement is the basis of RBI's accountability for inflation.
mcqs.topic: The Organisational Structure for Monetary Policy Decisions

mcqs.q: The inflation target notified by the Government is:
options: CPI inflation of 4% with a band of 2% to 6%
WPI inflation of 4% with a band of 2% to 6%
CPI inflation of 6% with a band of 4% to 8%
mcqs.explain: The Central Government notified a target of 4% CPI inflation with a tolerance band of 2% to 6%. 'WPI inflation' is the trap — India chose CPI because it reflects the cost of living and shapes inflation expectations better. In practice: market economists compare each month's CPI print with the 4% target and the 6% upper limit to anticipate the MPC's next move.
mcqs.topic: The Organisational Structure for Monetary Policy Decisions

mcqs.q: The inflation target is considered missed if average inflation is above the upper tolerance level for:
mcqs.explain: The target is deemed missed if average CPI inflation stays above the upper tolerance limit (6%) or below the lower limit (2%) for any three consecutive quarters. 'Any one quarter' is the trap — the framework allows temporary deviations. In practice: in 2022, inflation exceeded 6% for three straight quarters, and the RBI had to send a report to the government explaining the reasons and remedies.
mcqs.topic: The Organisational Structure for Monetary Policy Decisions

mcqs.q: The RBI must publish a Monetary Policy Report every:
mcqs.explain: Every six months the RBI is required to bring out a Monetary Policy Report that explains the sources of inflation and its forecasts for the next six to eighteen months. 'Every five years' is the trap — that is how often the government sets the inflation target, in consultation with the RBI. In practice: economists and bond analysts use the report's projections to forecast interest rates.
mcqs.topic: The Organisational Structure for Monetary Policy Decisions

mcqs.q: Which committee recommended making inflation targeting the primary objective of RBI's monetary policy?
options: Second Working Group on Money Supply
mcqs.explain: The Expert Committee headed by Urjit Patel (January 2014) advised the RBI to give up its multiple-indicator approach and to adopt inflation targeting as the main goal of monetary policy. The Narasimham Committee is the trap — it recommended banking-sector reforms and the LAF. In practice: its recommendations led to the 2016 RBI Act amendment, the MPC and the 4% CPI target.
mcqs.topic: The Organisational Structure for Monetary Policy Decisions

questions.q: The banking system's NDTL is ₹25,00,000 crore. With CRR at 3% and SLR at 18%, compute (a) the CRR balance, (b) the SLR holding, (c) funds available for lending. (d) If CRR is cut by 0.25 percentage point and the money multiplier is 4, what is the potential effect on money supply? (e) Name the policy direction.

model.text: (d) Released = 0.25% × 25,00,000 = ₹6,250 crore; potential money supply effect = 6,250 × 4 = ₹1,00,000 crore. (e) Expansionary (easy) monetary policy.

remarks: Present as a statement with "Less:" lines.
mistakes: Applying SLR to the amount left after CRR (both apply to NDTL).
tips: State that both ratios are percentages of NDTL.

checks.label: potential money supply effect at m = 4

questions.q: A bank needs ₹800 crore for 7 days. Compute the interest cost (₹ lakh, 365-day year) if borrowed (a) under repo at 5.25%, (b) under MSF at 5.50%, and (c) the extra cost of MSF. (d) Why does the RBI keep MSF above repo?

model.text: (d) MSF is a penal window for emergency overnight funds; keeping it above repo encourages banks to plan liquidity and borrow through regular LAF, and it caps overnight market rates (ceiling of the corridor).

tips: Show the formula: principal × rate × days/365.

questions.q: Quarterly average CPI inflation over six quarters was 1.9%, 1.7%, 1.8%, 5.9%, 6.3%, 6.6%. (a) State the inflation target and tolerance band. (b) Was there a failure in quarters 1–3? (c) In quarters 4–6? (d) What must the RBI do on failure?

model.text: (a) CPI 4%, band 2%–6%. (b) Quarters 1–3 all below 2% (average 1.8%) → three consecutive quarters below the lower tolerance → failure. (c) Quarter 4 (5.9%) is within the band, so only quarters 5 and 6 exceed 6% (three-quarter mean 6.27%) → no failure yet.
(d) The RBI must report to the Government the reasons for failure, the remedial actions proposed and the time within which the target will be achieved.

remarks: Failure can be on the LOW side too — many candidates forget this.
mistakes: Using the average of the three quarters instead of checking each quarter.
tips: Check each of the three consecutive quarters against the band.

summary: Monetary policy regulates availability, cost and use of money and credit; easing = lower rates; tightening = higher rates.

Framework: objectives (price stability with growth; RBI Act 1934 preamble), transmission (interest rate/saving–investment, cash flow, asset price & wealth, exchange rate, credit channels), operating procedure.

Quantitative tools: CRR 3% (cash with RBI), SLR 18% (liquid assets with bank), OMO (sell to absorb, buy to inject), MSS, bank rate (penalties), LAF — repo 5.25% (policy rate), reverse repo 3.35%, MSF 5.50%.
Qualitative tools: margin requirements, moral suasion, selective credit control.

Flexible inflation targeting: RBI Act amended (27 June 2016); MPFA; CPI 4% ± 2%; target set by Government every five years; failure = three consecutive quarters outside the band; Monetary Policy Report every six months.
MPC: six members (Governor, Deputy Governor, one RBI officer, three external), majority vote, Governor's casting vote.
Challenges in emerging markets: weak financial systems, poor market integration, external shocks, autonomy, fiscal–monetary coordination.
remember: Repo = RBI lends; reverse repo = RBI borrows.
MSF is 0.25 point above repo per current rates; older texts say ±1.
traps: RBI SELLS securities to fight inflation (absorbs liquidity) — buying injects liquidity.
CRR is with the RBI; SLR assets stay with the bank.
Failure also occurs if inflation stays BELOW 2% for three quarters.
The MPC decides by majority vote, not by the Governor alone.

viva.q: What is the difference between the repo rate and the reverse repo rate?
viva.model: The repo rate is the rate at which banks borrow short-term funds from the RBI by selling government securities with an agreement to buy them back; it injects liquidity and is the policy rate. The reverse repo rate is the rate at which the RBI borrows from banks, that is, the rate the RBI pays banks for parking surplus funds, which absorbs liquidity.

viva.q: Describe the Monetary Policy Committee and how it decides.
viva.model: The Monetary Policy Committee was set up under the RBI Act amended in 2016. It has six members: the RBI Governor as chairperson, the Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy, one RBI officer, and three external members appointed by the Central Government. It decides the policy repo rate needed to achieve the inflation target by majority vote, and the Governor has a casting vote in case of a tie.

points.pt: Governor chairs; three external members appointed by Government
Decides the policy (repo) rate by majority vote

viva.q: What is India's inflation target and when is it treated as a failure?
viva.model: The target is consumer price index inflation of four per cent, with an upper tolerance of six per cent and a lower tolerance of two per cent. It is a failure if average inflation stays above six per cent for three consecutive quarters, or below two per cent for three consecutive quarters.

points.pt: Failure: outside the band for three consecutive quarters

viva.q: Explain how a cut in the repo rate is transmitted to the economy.
viva.model: A repo rate cut lowers banks' cost of funds, so lending and deposit rates fall. Lower deposit rates reduce saving and lower loan rates encourage households to borrow and firms to invest. Lower EMIs leave people with more cash to spend. Lower rates also raise asset prices like shares and houses, increasing wealth and spending, and may weaken the rupee, helping exports. Overall demand and output rise, with some upward pressure on inflation.

points.pt: Lower lending/deposit rates → more borrowing and investment
Names at least two channels (cash flow / asset prices & wealth / exchange rate / saving)

viva.q: How does the RBI use open market operations to control inflation?
viva.model: To control inflation the RBI sells government securities in the open market. Banks and the public pay for them, so liquidity is absorbed, bank reserves fall and money supply and credit contract. To inject liquidity during a slowdown the RBI buys government securities instead.

cases.title: A tight week for Pragati Bank
cases.case: Pragati Bank has NDTL of ₹40,000 crore and has run short of funds after large advance-tax outflows. It needs ₹200 crore for one night. It can borrow under LAF repo at 5.25% using surplus government securities, or under MSF at 5.50% by dipping into its SLR holdings. The same week the MPC, citing CPI inflation of 6.4% for the third straight quarter, raises the repo rate.

mcqs.q: The one-night interest cost under repo (₹ lakh, 365-day year) is about:
mcqs.explain: Interest = 200 crore × 5.25% × 1 ÷ 365 = ₹0.02877 crore ≈ ₹2.88 lakh. Traps: 3.01 uses the MSF rate of 5.50%; 1.84 uses the reverse repo rate of 3.35%; 10.5 is a full year's interest in crore. In practice: Pragati Bank's treasury would choose repo over MSF, since it has surplus securities, saving about ₹0.13 lakh per night on ₹200 crore.

mcqs.q: Under MSF, Pragati Bank is:
options: Borrowing overnight at a penal rate by dipping into SLR securities
Lending surplus funds to the RBI
mcqs.explain: Under the Marginal Standing Facility, a bank borrows overnight from the RBI at a penal rate above repo, and may dip into its SLR securities within a permitted limit. 'Lending surplus funds to the RBI' is the trap — that is a reverse repo or deposit facility. In practice: banks resort to MSF when they lack surplus securities for repo, such as during large tax outflows in mid-March, June, September and December.

mcqs.q: With CPI at 6.4% for three straight quarters, the RBI has:
options: Failed to meet the inflation target and must report reasons and remedies to the Government
Missed the target only if inflation crosses 8%
No obligation as the target is advisory
mcqs.explain: CPI inflation of 6.4% is above the 6% upper tolerance limit for three consecutive quarters, which counts as failure to meet the target. The RBI must then report to the government the reasons for failure, remedial actions, and the expected time to return to target. 'Missed the target only if inflation crosses 8%' is the trap. In practice: the RBI sent exactly such a report to the government in November 2022.
mcqs.topic: The Organisational Structure for Monetary Policy Decisions

mcqs.q: The MPC's repo hike will, through the cash-flow channel:
options: Raise EMIs on floating-rate loans, leaving borrowers less cash to spend
mcqs.explain: Through the cash-flow channel, a repo hike raises interest rates on floating-rate loans linked to the benchmark, so EMIs rise and borrowers have less cash left for other spending, reducing demand. 'Lower EMIs' is the trap — that would follow a rate cut. In practice: most new retail loans in India are linked to the repo-based external benchmark rate, so hikes pass quickly to household budgets.
